lesson.title: There and Back: What Round Trip Time Tells You About a Network
lesson.summary: Round trip time is how long a packet takes to reach a destination and for a reply to return, and it is the delay metric most tools measure because it needs only one clock.
lesson.body:
Round trip time, almost always abbreviated RTT, is the time it takes for a small packet to travel from a source to a destination and for a reply to travel all the way back to the source. It is one of the most commonly measured quantities in networking, precisely because it can be measured from a single machine without needing to compare clocks with the remote device.

The classic way to measure RTT is the ping utility, which sends an ICMP echo request packet to a destination and times how long it takes for the echo reply to return. Because both the timestamp for sending and the timestamp for receiving are taken on the same machine, using the same clock, there is no need to synchronize clocks between two different hosts the way you would if you tried to measure one way latency directly. This practical convenience is a big reason RTT, rather than one way delay, is the number reported by most everyday network tools.

If a path is symmetric, meaning the outbound and return trips pass through the same links and routers, RTT is approximately twice the one way latency covered earlier in this sequence, since the packet pays each delay component, propagation, transmission, queuing, and processing, once going out and once coming back. In practice, paths are often not perfectly symmetric. Internet routing can send traffic out through one set of links and back through a different set, so RTT is only a rough proxy for one way latency rather than an exact doubling of it.

As a concrete example, if you ping a web server and see a reported time of 40 milliseconds, a reasonable rough estimate is that the one way latency in each direction is around 20 milliseconds, assuming symmetric routing. Distance matters enormously here. A geostationary satellite link has a one way propagation delay of roughly 250 milliseconds, because the signal has to travel about 35,786 kilometers up to the satellite and the same distance back down, close to the speed of light. Round trip time over such a link is therefore around 500 milliseconds from propagation alone, before adding any transmission, queuing, or processing delay, which explains why satellite internet feels noticeably laggy even when bandwidth is decent.

RTT shows up throughout networking protocols, not just in diagnostic tools. TCP measures RTT continuously during a connection to calculate its retransmission timeout, the amount of time it waits before assuming a packet was lost and resending it. TCP's initial three way handshake, used to establish a connection, also costs at least one full RTT before any application data can be sent, which is part of why connection setup time matters for short lived web requests.

RTT is best understood as the same delay components covered so far in this chapter sequence, transmission delay, queuing delay, and processing delay, plus propagation delay, all experienced twice: once on the way to the destination and once on the way back. A later chapter builds directly on RTT to introduce the bandwidth delay product, a quantity that combines RTT with link bandwidth to describe how much data can be in flight on a connection at once.
